case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s presented with a 20-year history of intermittent tender papules and nodules that were localized to the medial surface of her labia majora and labia minora. Purulent drainage was often reported from the lesions. The lesions were episodic and did not recur in the same locations. Flares occurred with inconsistent frequency, sometimes coinciding with the mid menstrual cycle. She denied lesions occurring on the hair-bearing labia majora or buttocks. Physical examination revealed an erythematous papule on the right medial labium minus (Figure 1) and an erythematous nodule on the left lateral labium minus. Surface swabs of the lesions were obtained for aerobic culture and herpes simplex virus (HSV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR). A 4-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained from the left lateral labium minus for histopathological examination.
case_info.caption: Erythematous papule on the medial surface of the right labium minus.
case_info.explanation: Histology revealed spongiosis with neutrophils in the epidermis, while the dermis showed diffuse neutrophilic infiltration. There was inflammation surrounding sebaceous glands and neutrophils focally noted within the sebaceous gland epithelium. Special stains for infection also yielded negative results. Results of the HSV PCR and aerobic culture were also negative. Given these findings, the patient received a diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis. The patient had undergone numerous treatments before presentation and after a diagnosis was rendered for prophylaxis of flares and short-term management of flares. This included clindamycin, 1%, gel, mupirocin ointment, topical compounded spironolactone, clascoterone cream, and the following oral agents: doxycycline, minocycline, sarecycline, cephalexin, amoxicillin/clavulanate, and spironolactone. She found the minocycline and the amoxicillin/clavulanate to be the most effective oral medications. Mupirocin ointment provided mild relief during flares. Unfortunately, she did not experience improvement while taking spironolactone, 25 mg, daily and was unable to tolerate a higher dose due to hypotension. Due to her history of migraines, her neurologist had advised her not to take combined oral contraceptives. She declined treatment with isotretinoin and drospirenone-only oral contraceptives. Characterized by inflammation of the sebaceous glands of the vulva (Figure 2), vulvar sebaceous adenitis was first reported in 2014.1Other names for this disease entity include genital neutrophilic sebaceous adenitis and vulvar Fordyce adenitis.2,3Occurring in premenopausal adult women, clinical manifestations include recurrent tender papules, pustules, or nodules affecting the labia minora and, less commonly, the medial aspect of the labia majora.1-4Suppuration of lesions and pitted scars have also been described. Vulvar sebaceous adenitis has often been reported to flare during the late luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.1-4Given the timing of exacerbations in many patients, in addition to it affecting women between puberty and menopause, the condition points toward having a hormonal effect. Known treatment options that can be associated with improvement or complete remission of symptoms include antiandrogens and the tetracycline class of antibiotics.1-4The latter is used for its anti-inflammatory properties rather than its antimicrobial effects.1,2In what is to our knowledge the largest cohort published to date,3zinc and isotretinoin additionally showed complete remission for several patients. However, the authors acknowledged that the improvement with oral zinc cannot definitively be attributed to the medication alone.3Although these treatments may be associated with complete remission and improvement for many patients, they also have been reported to have no effect for others.1,3 Histologically, sebaceous adenitis is characterized by dense neutrophilic inflammation that is centered around the sebaceous unit. Infectious studies are negative, and no viral cytopathic change is present. The diagnosis requires clinical correlation. The differential diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis includes hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), HSV, vulvar syringomas, and hidradenoma papilliferum. Histopathological examination and HSV PCR are helpful at narrowing the differential diagnosis. HS clinically presents as recurrent inflamed nodules, abscesses, and fistulae that occur on hair-bearing skin of the axillary, inguinal, inframammary, vulvar, and gluteal regions. HS is diagnosed clinically, and histologic confirmation is typically unnecessary. However, if performed, histology of HS is characterized by follicular hyperkeratosis and subsequent inflammation of apocrine glands.5A key distinguishing clinical feature between HS and vulvar sebaceous adenitis is the anatomical location affected: HS occurs on the hair-bearing aspect of the labia majora, while vulvar sebaceous adenitis occurs on the mucosal surfaces of the labia majora and labia minora. Genital HSV is an infection that typically presents with painful vesicles or erosions on the anogenital area. The virus can remain dormant and shed asymptomatically or recur as outbreaks during the individual’s lifetime. There are numerous ways to test for HSV, with PCR being the standard molecular diagnosis technique. Histology results show vesicle formation with viral cytopathic change, multinucleated giant cells, molding of cells together, and chromatin margination.6 Syringomas are benign adnexal tumors that present as flesh-colored papules. The papules most commonly occur periorbitally, but also rarely occur on the vulva. The lesions may be pruritic or asymptomatic and are thus found incidentally. Vulvar syringomas are diagnosed via skin biopsy specimens, with microscopy revealing sweat ductlike glandular structures.7Symptomatic presentation of tenderness and cyclical patterns are key clinical characteristics that distinguish vulvar sebaceous adenitis from vulvar syringomas.

This condition often presents with similar symptoms in areas like the labia and can lead to recurrent abscess formation. The chronicity and localization of the symptoms align well with this diagnosis, making it a leading consideration while waiting for biopsy and culture results.

We should await the biopsy results to differentiate these conditions definitively.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s presented with a 20-year history of intermittent tender papules and nodules that were localized to the medial surface of her labia majora and labia minora. Purulent drainage was often reported from the lesions. The lesions were episodic and did not recur in the same locations. Flares occurred with inconsistent frequency, sometimes coinciding with the mid menstrual cycle. She denied lesions occurring on the hair-bearing labia majora or buttocks. Physical examination revealed an erythematous papule on the right medial labium minus (Figure 1) and an erythematous nodule on the left lateral labium minus. Surface swabs of the lesions were obtained for aerobic culture and herpes simplex virus (HSV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR). A 4-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained from the left lateral labium minus for histopathological examination.
case_info.caption: Erythematous papule on the medial surface of the right labium minus.
case_info.explanation: Histology revealed spongiosis with neutrophils in the epidermis, while the dermis showed diffuse neutrophilic infiltration. There was inflammation surrounding sebaceous glands and neutrophils focally noted within the sebaceous gland epithelium. Special stains for infection also yielded negative results. Results of the HSV PCR and aerobic culture were also negative. Given these findings, the patient received a diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis. The patient had undergone numerous treatments before presentation and after a diagnosis was rendered for prophylaxis of flares and short-term management of flares. This included clindamycin, 1%, gel, mupirocin ointment, topical compounded spironolactone, clascoterone cream, and the following oral agents: doxycycline, minocycline, sarecycline, cephalexin, amoxicillin/clavulanate, and spironolactone. She found the minocycline and the amoxicillin/clavulanate to be the most effective oral medications. Mupirocin ointment provided mild relief during flares. Unfortunately, she did not experience improvement while taking spironolactone, 25 mg, daily and was unable to tolerate a higher dose due to hypotension. Due to her history of migraines, her neurologist had advised her not to take combined oral contraceptives. She declined treatment with isotretinoin and drospirenone-only oral contraceptives. Characterized by inflammation of the sebaceous glands of the vulva (Figure 2), vulvar sebaceous adenitis was first reported in 2014.1Other names for this disease entity include genital neutrophilic sebaceous adenitis and vulvar Fordyce adenitis.2,3Occurring in premenopausal adult women, clinical manifestations include recurrent tender papules, pustules, or nodules affecting the labia minora and, less commonly, the medial aspect of the labia majora.1-4Suppuration of lesions and pitted scars have also been described. Vulvar sebaceous adenitis has often been reported to flare during the late luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.1-4Given the timing of exacerbations in many patients, in addition to it affecting women between puberty and menopause, the condition points toward having a hormonal effect. Known treatment options that can be associated with improvement or complete remission of symptoms include antiandrogens and the tetracycline class of antibiotics.1-4The latter is used for its anti-inflammatory properties rather than its antimicrobial effects.1,2In what is to our knowledge the largest cohort published to date,3zinc and isotretinoin additionally showed complete remission for several patients. However, the authors acknowledged that the improvement with oral zinc cannot definitively be attributed to the medication alone.3Although these treatments may be associated with complete remission and improvement for many patients, they also have been reported to have no effect for others.1,3 Histologically, sebaceous adenitis is characterized by dense neutrophilic inflammation that is centered around the sebaceous unit. Infectious studies are negative, and no viral cytopathic change is present. The diagnosis requires clinical correlation. The differential diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis includes hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), HSV, vulvar syringomas, and hidradenoma papilliferum. Histopathological examination and HSV PCR are helpful at narrowing the differential diagnosis. HS clinically presents as recurrent inflamed nodules, abscesses, and fistulae that occur on hair-bearing skin of the axillary, inguinal, inframammary, vulvar, and gluteal regions. HS is diagnosed clinically, and histologic confirmation is typically unnecessary. However, if performed, histology of HS is characterized by follicular hyperkeratosis and subsequent inflammation of apocrine glands.5A key distinguishing clinical feature between HS and vulvar sebaceous adenitis is the anatomical location affected: HS occurs on the hair-bearing aspect of the labia majora, while vulvar sebaceous adenitis occurs on the mucosal surfaces of the labia majora and labia minora. Genital HSV is an infection that typically presents with painful vesicles or erosions on the anogenital area. The virus can remain dormant and shed asymptomatically or recur as outbreaks during the individual’s lifetime. There are numerous ways to test for HSV, with PCR being the standard molecular diagnosis technique. Histology results show vesicle formation with viral cytopathic change, multinucleated giant cells, molding of cells together, and chromatin margination.6 Syringomas are benign adnexal tumors that present as flesh-colored papules. The papules most commonly occur periorbitally, but also rarely occur on the vulva. The lesions may be pruritic or asymptomatic and are thus found incidentally. Vulvar syringomas are diagnosed via skin biopsy specimens, with microscopy revealing sweat ductlike glandular structures.7Symptomatic presentation of tenderness and cyclical patterns are key clinical characteristics that distinguish vulvar sebaceous adenitis from vulvar syringomas.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Flares occurred with inconsistent frequency, sometimes coinciding with the mid menstrual cycle. She denied lesions occurring on the hair-bearing labia majora or buttocks. Physical examination revealed an erythematous papule on the right medial labium minus (Figure 1) and an erythematous nodule on the left lateral labium minus. Surface swabs of the lesions were obtained for aerobic culture and herpes simplex virus (HSV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR). case_info.caption: Erythematous papule on the medial surface of the right labium minus.
case_info.explanation: Histology revealed spongiosis with neutrophils in the epidermis, while the dermis showed diffuse neutrophilic infiltration. There was inflammation surrounding sebaceous glands and neutrophils focally noted within the sebaceous gland epithelium. Special stains for infection also yielded negative results. Results of the HSV PCR and aerobic culture were also negative. Given these findings, the patient received a diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis. The patient had undergone numerous treatments before presentation and after a diagnosis was rendered for prophylaxis of flares and short-term management of flares. This included clindamycin, 1%, gel, mupirocin ointment, topical compounded spironolactone, clascoterone cream, and the following oral agents: doxycycline, minocycline, sarecycline, cephalexin, amoxicillin/clavulanate, and spironolactone. She found the minocycline and the amoxicillin/clavulanate to be the most effective oral medications. Mupirocin ointment provided mild relief during flares. Unfortunately, she did not experience improvement while taking spironolactone, 25 mg, daily and was unable to tolerate a higher dose due to hypotension. Due to her history of migraines, her neurologist had advised her not to take combined oral contraceptives. She declined treatment with isotretinoin and drospirenone-only oral contraceptives. Characterized by inflammation of the sebaceous glands of the vulva (Figure 2), vulvar sebaceous adenitis was first reported in 2014.1Other names for this disease entity include genital neutrophilic sebaceous adenitis and vulvar Fordyce adenitis.2,3Occurring in premenopausal adult women, clinical manifestations include recurrent tender papules, pustules, or nodules affecting the labia minora and, less commonly, the medial aspect of the labia majora.1-4Suppuration of lesions and pitted scars have also been described. Vulvar sebaceous adenitis has often been reported to flare during the late luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.1-4Given the timing of exacerbations in many patients, in addition to it affecting women between puberty and menopause, the condition points toward having a hormonal effect. Known treatment options that can be associated with improvement or complete remission of symptoms include antiandrogens and the tetracycline class of antibiotics.1-4The latter is used for its anti-inflammatory properties rather than its antimicrobial effects.1,2In what is to our knowledge the largest cohort published to date,3zinc and isotretinoin additionally showed complete remission for several patients. However, the authors acknowledged that the improvement with oral zinc cannot definitively be attributed to the medication alone.3Although these treatments may be associated with complete remission and improvement for many patients, they also have been reported to have no effect for others.1,3 Histologically, sebaceous adenitis is characterized by dense neutrophilic inflammation that is centered around the sebaceous unit. Infectious studies are negative, and no viral cytopathic change is present. The diagnosis requires clinical correlation. The differential diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis includes hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), HSV, vulvar syringomas, and hidradenoma papilliferum. Histopathological examination and HSV PCR are helpful at narrowing the differential diagnosis. HS clinically presents as recurrent inflamed nodules, abscesses, and fistulae that occur on hair-bearing skin of the axillary, inguinal, inframammary, vulvar, and gluteal regions. HS is diagnosed clinically, and histologic confirmation is typically unnecessary. However, if performed, histology of HS is characterized by follicular hyperkeratosis and subsequent inflammation of apocrine glands.5A key distinguishing clinical feature between HS and vulvar sebaceous adenitis is the anatomical location affected: HS occurs on the hair-bearing aspect of the labia majora, while vulvar sebaceous adenitis occurs on the mucosal surfaces of the labia majora and labia minora. Genital HSV is an infection that typically presents with painful vesicles or erosions on the anogenital area. The virus can remain dormant and shed asymptomatically or recur as outbreaks during the individual’s lifetime. There are numerous ways to test for HSV, with PCR being the standard molecular diagnosis technique. Histology results show vesicle formation with viral cytopathic change, multinucleated giant cells, molding of cells together, and chromatin margination.6 Syringomas are benign adnexal tumors that present as flesh-colored papules. The papules most commonly occur periorbitally, but also rarely occur on the vulva. The lesions may be pruritic or asymptomatic and are thus found incidentally. Vulvar syringomas are diagnosed via skin biopsy specimens, with microscopy revealing sweat ductlike glandular structures.7Symptomatic presentation of tenderness and cyclical patterns are key clinical characteristics that distinguish vulvar sebaceous adenitis from vulvar syringomas.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort

   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's

   Scoring:

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

Physical examination revealed an erythematous papule on the right medial labium minus (Figure 1) and an erythematous nodule on the left lateral labium minus. case_info.caption: Erythematous papule on the medial surface of the right labium minus.
case_info.explanation: Histology revealed spongiosis with neutrophils in the epidermis, while the dermis showed diffuse neutrophilic infiltration. There was inflammation surrounding sebaceous glands and neutrophils focally noted within the sebaceous gland epithelium. Special stains for infection also yielded negative results. Results of the HSV PCR and aerobic culture were also negative. Given these findings, the patient received a diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis. The patient had undergone numerous treatments before presentation and after a diagnosis was rendered for prophylaxis of flares and short-term management of flares. This included clindamycin, 1%, gel, mupirocin ointment, topical compounded spironolactone, clascoterone cream, and the following oral agents: doxycycline, minocycline, sarecycline, cephalexin, amoxicillin/clavulanate, and spironolactone. She found the minocycline and the amoxicillin/clavulanate to be the most effective oral medications. Mupirocin ointment provided mild relief during flares. Unfortunately, she did not experience improvement while taking spironolactone, 25 mg, daily and was unable to tolerate a higher dose due to hypotension. Due to her history of migraines, her neurologist had advised her not to take combined oral contraceptives. She declined treatment with isotretinoin and drospirenone-only oral contraceptives. Characterized by inflammation of the sebaceous glands of the vulva (Figure 2), vulvar sebaceous adenitis was first reported in 2014.1Other names for this disease entity include genital neutrophilic sebaceous adenitis and vulvar Fordyce adenitis.2,3Occurring in premenopausal adult women, clinical manifestations include recurrent tender papules, pustules, or nodules affecting the labia minora and, less commonly, the medial aspect of the labia majora.1-4Suppuration of lesions and pitted scars have also been described. Vulvar sebaceous adenitis has often been reported to flare during the late luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.1-4Given the timing of exacerbations in many patients, in addition to it affecting women between puberty and menopause, the condition points toward having a hormonal effect. Known treatment options that can be associated with improvement or complete remission of symptoms include antiandrogens and the tetracycline class of antibiotics.1-4The latter is used for its anti-inflammatory properties rather than its antimicrobial effects.1,2In what is to our knowledge the largest cohort published to date,3zinc and isotretinoin additionally showed complete remission for several patients. However, the authors acknowledged that the improvement with oral zinc cannot definitively be attributed to the medication alone.3Although these treatments may be associated with complete remission and improvement for many patients, they also have been reported to have no effect for others.1,3 Histologically, sebaceous adenitis is characterized by dense neutrophilic inflammation that is centered around the sebaceous unit. Infectious studies are negative, and no viral cytopathic change is present. The diagnosis requires clinical correlation. The differential diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis includes hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), HSV, vulvar syringomas, and hidradenoma papilliferum. Histopathological examination and HSV PCR are helpful at narrowing the differential diagnosis. HS clinically presents as recurrent inflamed nodules, abscesses, and fistulae that occur on hair-bearing skin of the axillary, inguinal, inframammary, vulvar, and gluteal regions. HS is diagnosed clinically, and histologic confirmation is typically unnecessary. However, if performed, histology of HS is characterized by follicular hyperkeratosis and subsequent inflammation of apocrine glands.5A key distinguishing clinical feature between HS and vulvar sebaceous adenitis is the anatomical location affected: HS occurs on the hair-bearing aspect of the labia majora, while vulvar sebaceous adenitis occurs on the mucosal surfaces of the labia majora and labia minora. Genital HSV is an infection that typically presents with painful vesicles or erosions on the anogenital area. The virus can remain dormant and shed asymptomatically or recur as outbreaks during the individual’s lifetime. There are numerous ways to test for HSV, with PCR being the standard molecular diagnosis technique. Histology results show vesicle formation with viral cytopathic change, multinucleated giant cells, molding of cells together, and chromatin margination.6 Syringomas are benign adnexal tumors that present as flesh-colored papules. The papules most commonly occur periorbitally, but also rarely occur on the vulva. The lesions may be pruritic or asymptomatic and are thus found incidentally. Vulvar syringomas are diagnosed via skin biopsy specimens, with microscopy revealing sweat ductlike glandular structures.7Symptomatic presentation of tenderness and cyclical patterns are key clinical characteristics that distinguish vulvar sebaceous adenitis from vulvar syringomas.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s presented with a 20-year history of intermittent tender papules and nodules that were localized to the medial surface of her labia majora and labia minora. Purulent drainage was often reported from the lesions. The lesions were episodic and did not recur in the same locations. Flares occurred with inconsistent frequency, sometimes coinciding with the mid menstrual cycle. She denied lesions occurring on the hair-bearing labia majora or buttocks. Physical examination revealed an erythematous papule on the right medial labium minus (Figure 1) and an erythematous nodule on the left lateral labium minus. Surface swabs of the lesions were obtained for aerobic culture and herpes simplex virus (HSV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR). A 4-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained from the left lateral labium minus for histopathological examination.
case_info.caption: Erythematous papule on the medial surface of the right labium minus.
case_info.explanation: Histology revealed spongiosis with neutrophils in the epidermis, while the dermis showed diffuse neutrophilic infiltration. There was inflammation surrounding sebaceous glands and neutrophils focally noted within the sebaceous gland epithelium. Special stains for infection also yielded negative results. Results of the HSV PCR and aerobic culture were also negative. Given these findings, the patient received a diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis. The patient had undergone numerous treatments before presentation and after a diagnosis was rendered for prophylaxis of flares and short-term management of flares. This included clindamycin, 1%, gel, mupirocin ointment, topical compounded spironolactone, clascoterone cream, and the following oral agents: doxycycline, minocycline, sarecycline, cephalexin, amoxicillin/clavulanate, and spironolactone. She found the minocycline and the amoxicillin/clavulanate to be the most effective oral medications. Mupirocin ointment provided mild relief during flares. Unfortunately, she did not experience improvement while taking spironolactone, 25 mg, daily and was unable to tolerate a higher dose due to hypotension. Due to her history of migraines, her neurologist had advised her not to take combined oral contraceptives. She declined treatment with isotretinoin and drospirenone-only oral contraceptives. Characterized by inflammation of the sebaceous glands of the vulva (Figure 2), vulvar sebaceous adenitis was first reported in 2014.1Other names for this disease entity include genital neutrophilic sebaceous adenitis and vulvar Fordyce adenitis.2,3Occurring in premenopausal adult women, clinical manifestations include recurrent tender papules, pustules, or nodules affecting the labia minora and, less commonly, the medial aspect of the labia majora.1-4Suppuration of lesions and pitted scars have also been described. Vulvar sebaceous adenitis has often been reported to flare during the late luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.1-4Given the timing of exacerbations in many patients, in addition to it affecting women between puberty and menopause, the condition points toward having a hormonal effect. Known treatment options that can be associated with improvement or complete remission of symptoms include antiandrogens and the tetracycline class of antibiotics.1-4The latter is used for its anti-inflammatory properties rather than its antimicrobial effects.1,2In what is to our knowledge the largest cohort published to date,3zinc and isotretinoin additionally showed complete remission for several patients. However, the authors acknowledged that the improvement with oral zinc cannot definitively be attributed to the medication alone.3Although these treatments may be associated with complete remission and improvement for many patients, they also have been reported to have no effect for others.1,3 Histologically, sebaceous adenitis is characterized by dense neutrophilic inflammation that is centered around the sebaceous unit. Infectious studies are negative, and no viral cytopathic change is present. The diagnosis requires clinical correlation. The differential diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis includes hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), HSV, vulvar syringomas, and hidradenoma papilliferum. Histopathological examination and HSV PCR are helpful at narrowing the differential diagnosis. HS clinically presents as recurrent inflamed nodules, abscesses, and fistulae that occur on hair-bearing skin of the axillary, inguinal, inframammary, vulvar, and gluteal regions. HS is diagnosed clinically, and histologic confirmation is typically unnecessary. However, if performed, histology of HS is characterized by follicular hyperkeratosis and subsequent inflammation of apocrine glands.5A key distinguishing clinical feature between HS and vulvar sebaceous adenitis is the anatomical location affected: HS occurs on the hair-bearing aspect of the labia majora, while vulvar sebaceous adenitis occurs on the mucosal surfaces of the labia majora and labia minora. Genital HSV is an infection that typically presents with painful vesicles or erosions on the anogenital area. The virus can remain dormant and shed asymptomatically or recur as outbreaks during the individual’s lifetime. There are numerous ways to test for HSV, with PCR being the standard molecular diagnosis technique. Histology results show vesicle formation with viral cytopathic change, multinucleated giant cells, molding of cells together, and chromatin margination.6 Syringomas are benign adnexal tumors that present as flesh-colored papules. The papules most commonly occur periorbitally, but also rarely occur on the vulva. The lesions may be pruritic or asymptomatic and are thus found incidentally. Vulvar syringomas are diagnosed via skin biopsy specimens, with microscopy revealing sweat ductlike glandular structures.7Symptomatic presentation of tenderness and cyclical patterns are key clinical characteristics that distinguish vulvar sebaceous adenitis from vulvar syringomas.

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Case]

Surface swabs of the lesions were obtained for aerobic culture and herpes simplex virus (HSV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR). A 4-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained from the left lateral labium minus for histopathological examination.

[Persona]

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 9.1. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Purulent drainage was often reported from the lesions. The lesions were episodic and did not recur in the same locations. Flares occurred with inconsistent frequency, sometimes coinciding with the mid menstrual cycle. She denied lesions occurring on the hair-bearing labia majora or buttocks. Physical examination revealed an erythematous papule on the right medial labium minus (Figure 1) and an erythematous nodule on the left lateral labium minus. Surface swabs of the lesions were obtained for aerobic culture and herpes simplex virus (HSV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR). A 4-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained from the left lateral labium minus for histopathological examination.
case_info.caption: Erythematous papule on the medial surface of the right labium minus.
case_info.explanation: Histology revealed spongiosis with neutrophils in the epidermis, while the dermis showed diffuse neutrophilic infiltration. There was inflammation surrounding sebaceous glands and neutrophils focally noted within the sebaceous gland epithelium. Special stains for infection also yielded negative results. Results of the HSV PCR and aerobic culture were also negative. Given these findings, the patient received a diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis. The patient had undergone numerous treatments before presentation and after a diagnosis was rendered for prophylaxis of flares and short-term management of flares. This included clindamycin, 1%, gel, mupirocin ointment, topical compounded spironolactone, clascoterone cream, and the following oral agents: doxycycline, minocycline, sarecycline, cephalexin, amoxicillin/clavulanate, and spironolactone. She found the minocycline and the amoxicillin/clavulanate to be the most effective oral medications. Mupirocin ointment provided mild relief during flares. Unfortunately, she did not experience improvement while taking spironolactone, 25 mg, daily and was unable to tolerate a higher dose due to hypotension. Due to her history of migraines, her neurologist had advised her not to take combined oral contraceptives. She declined treatment with isotretinoin and drospirenone-only oral contraceptives. Characterized by inflammation of the sebaceous glands of the vulva (Figure 2), vulvar sebaceous adenitis was first reported in 2014.1Other names for this disease entity include genital neutrophilic sebaceous adenitis and vulvar Fordyce adenitis.2,3Occurring in premenopausal adult women, clinical manifestations include recurrent tender papules, pustules, or nodules affecting the labia minora and, less commonly, the medial aspect of the labia majora.1-4Suppuration of lesions and pitted scars have also been described. Vulvar sebaceous adenitis has often been reported to flare during the late luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.1-4Given the timing of exacerbations in many patients, in addition to it affecting women between puberty and menopause, the condition points toward having a hormonal effect. Known treatment options that can be associated with improvement or complete remission of symptoms include antiandrogens and the tetracycline class of antibiotics.1-4The latter is used for its anti-inflammatory properties rather than its antimicrobial effects.1,2In what is to our knowledge the largest cohort published to date,3zinc and isotretinoin additionally showed complete remission for several patients. However, the authors acknowledged that the improvement with oral zinc cannot definitively be attributed to the medication alone.3Although these treatments may be associated with complete remission and improvement for many patients, they also have been reported to have no effect for others.1,3 Histologically, sebaceous adenitis is characterized by dense neutrophilic inflammation that is centered around the sebaceous unit. Infectious studies are negative, and no viral cytopathic change is present. The diagnosis requires clinical correlation. The differential diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis includes hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), HSV, vulvar syringomas, and hidradenoma papilliferum. Histopathological examination and HSV PCR are helpful at narrowing the differential diagnosis. HS clinically presents as recurrent inflamed nodules, abscesses, and fistulae that occur on hair-bearing skin of the axillary, inguinal, inframammary, vulvar, and gluteal regions. HS is diagnosed clinically, and histologic confirmation is typically unnecessary. However, if performed, histology of HS is characterized by follicular hyperkeratosis and subsequent inflammation of apocrine glands.5A key distinguishing clinical feature between HS and vulvar sebaceous adenitis is the anatomical location affected: HS occurs on the hair-bearing aspect of the labia majora, while vulvar sebaceous adenitis occurs on the mucosal surfaces of the labia majora and labia minora. Genital HSV is an infection that typically presents with painful vesicles or erosions on the anogenital area. The virus can remain dormant and shed asymptomatically or recur as outbreaks during the individual’s lifetime. There are numerous ways to test for HSV, with PCR being the standard molecular diagnosis technique. Histology results show vesicle formation with viral cytopathic change, multinucleated giant cells, molding of cells together, and chromatin margination.6 Syringomas are benign adnexal tumors that present as flesh-colored papules. The papules most commonly occur periorbitally, but also rarely occur on the vulva. The lesions may be pruritic or asymptomatic and are thus found incidentally. Vulvar syringomas are diagnosed via skin biopsy specimens, with microscopy revealing sweat ductlike glandular structures.7Symptomatic presentation of tenderness and cyclical patterns are key clinical characteristics that distinguish vulvar sebaceous adenitis from vulvar syringomas.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s presented with a 20-year history of intermittent tender papules and nodules that were localized to the medial surface of her labia majora and labia minora. Purulent drainage was often reported from the lesions. The lesions were episodic and did not recur in the same locations. Flares occurred with inconsistent frequency, sometimes coinciding with the mid menstrual cycle. She denied lesions occurring on the hair-bearing labia majora or buttocks. Physical examination revealed an erythematous papule on the right medial labium minus (Figure 1) and an erythematous nodule on the left lateral labium minus. Surface swabs of the lesions were obtained for aerobic culture and herpes simplex virus (HSV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR). A 4-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained from the left lateral labium minus for histopathological examination.
case_info.caption: Erythematous papule on the medial surface of the right labium minus.
case_info.explanation: Histology revealed spongiosis with neutrophils in the epidermis, while the dermis showed diffuse neutrophilic infiltration. There was inflammation surrounding sebaceous glands and neutrophils focally noted within the sebaceous gland epithelium. Special stains for infection also yielded negative results. Results of the HSV PCR and aerobic culture were also negative. Given these findings, the patient received a diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis. The patient had undergone numerous treatments before presentation and after a diagnosis was rendered for prophylaxis of flares and short-term management of flares. This included clindamycin, 1%, gel, mupirocin ointment, topical compounded spironolactone, clascoterone cream, and the following oral agents: doxycycline, minocycline, sarecycline, cephalexin, amoxicillin/clavulanate, and spironolactone. She found the minocycline and the amoxicillin/clavulanate to be the most effective oral medications. Mupirocin ointment provided mild relief during flares. Unfortunately, she did not experience improvement while taking spironolactone, 25 mg, daily and was unable to tolerate a higher dose due to hypotension. Due to her history of migraines, her neurologist had advised her not to take combined oral contraceptives. She declined treatment with isotretinoin and drospirenone-only oral contraceptives. Characterized by inflammation of the sebaceous glands of the vulva (Figure 2), vulvar sebaceous adenitis was first reported in 2014.1Other names for this disease entity include genital neutrophilic sebaceous adenitis and vulvar Fordyce adenitis.2,3Occurring in premenopausal adult women, clinical manifestations include recurrent tender papules, pustules, or nodules affecting the labia minora and, less commonly, the medial aspect of the labia majora.1-4Suppuration of lesions and pitted scars have also been described. Vulvar sebaceous adenitis has often been reported to flare during the late luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.1-4Given the timing of exacerbations in many patients, in addition to it affecting women between puberty and menopause, the condition points toward having a hormonal effect. Known treatment options that can be associated with improvement or complete remission of symptoms include antiandrogens and the tetracycline class of antibiotics.1-4The latter is used for its anti-inflammatory properties rather than its antimicrobial effects.1,2In what is to our knowledge the largest cohort published to date,3zinc and isotretinoin additionally showed complete remission for several patients. However, the authors acknowledged that the improvement with oral zinc cannot definitively be attributed to the medication alone.3Although these treatments may be associated with complete remission and improvement for many patients, they also have been reported to have no effect for others.1,3 Histologically, sebaceous adenitis is characterized by dense neutrophilic inflammation that is centered around the sebaceous unit. Infectious studies are negative, and no viral cytopathic change is present. The diagnosis requires clinical correlation. The differential diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis includes hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), HSV, vulvar syringomas, and hidradenoma papilliferum. Histopathological examination and HSV PCR are helpful at narrowing the differential diagnosis. HS clinically presents as recurrent inflamed nodules, abscesses, and fistulae that occur on hair-bearing skin of the axillary, inguinal, inframammary, vulvar, and gluteal regions. HS is diagnosed clinically, and histologic confirmation is typically unnecessary. However, if performed, histology of HS is characterized by follicular hyperkeratosis and subsequent inflammation of apocrine glands.5A key distinguishing clinical feature between HS and vulvar sebaceous adenitis is the anatomical location affected: HS occurs on the hair-bearing aspect of the labia majora, while vulvar sebaceous adenitis occurs on the mucosal surfaces of the labia majora and labia minora. Genital HSV is an infection that typically presents with painful vesicles or erosions on the anogenital area. The virus can remain dormant and shed asymptomatically or recur as outbreaks during the individual’s lifetime. There are numerous ways to test for HSV, with PCR being the standard molecular diagnosis technique. Histology results show vesicle formation with viral cytopathic change, multinucleated giant cells, molding of cells together, and chromatin margination.6 Syringomas are benign adnexal tumors that present as flesh-colored papules. The papules most commonly occur periorbitally, but also rarely occur on the vulva. The lesions may be pruritic or asymptomatic and are thus found incidentally. Vulvar syringomas are diagnosed via skin biopsy specimens, with microscopy revealing sweat ductlike glandular structures.7Symptomatic presentation of tenderness and cyclical patterns are key clinical characteristics that distinguish vulvar sebaceous adenitis from vulvar syringomas.

case_info.explanation: Histology revealed spongiosis with neutrophils in the epidermis, while the dermis showed diffuse neutrophilic infiltration. There was inflammation surrounding sebaceous glands and neutrophils focally noted within the sebaceous gland epithelium. Special stains for infection also yielded negative results. Results of the HSV PCR and aerobic culture were also negative. Given these findings, the patient received a diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis. The patient had undergone numerous treatments before presentation and after a diagnosis was rendered for prophylaxis of flares and short-term management of flares. This included clindamycin, 1%, gel, mupirocin ointment, topical compounded spironolactone, clascoterone cream, and the following oral agents: doxycycline, minocycline, sarecycline, cephalexin, amoxicillin/clavulanate, and spironolactone. She found the minocycline and the amoxicillin/clavulanate to be the most effective oral medications. Mupirocin ointment provided mild relief during flares. Unfortunately, she did not experience improvement while taking spironolactone, 25 mg, daily and was unable to tolerate a higher dose due to hypotension. Due to her history of migraines, her neurologist had advised her not to take combined oral contraceptives. She declined treatment with isotretinoin and drospirenone-only oral contraceptives. Characterized by inflammation of the sebaceous glands of the vulva (Figure 2), vulvar sebaceous adenitis was first reported in 2014.1Other names for this disease entity include genital neutrophilic sebaceous adenitis and vulvar Fordyce adenitis.2,3Occurring in premenopausal adult women, clinical manifestations include recurrent tender papules, pustules, or nodules affecting the labia minora and, less commonly, the medial aspect of the labia majora.1-4Suppuration of lesions and pitted scars have also been described. Vulvar sebaceous adenitis has often been reported to flare during the late luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.1-4Given the timing of exacerbations in many patients, in addition to it affecting women between puberty and menopause, the condition points toward having a hormonal effect. Known treatment options that can be associated with improvement or complete remission of symptoms include antiandrogens and the tetracycline class of antibiotics.1-4The latter is used for its anti-inflammatory properties rather than its antimicrobial effects.1,2In what is to our knowledge the largest cohort published to date,3zinc and isotretinoin additionally showed complete remission for several patients. However, the authors acknowledged that the improvement with oral zinc cannot definitively be attributed to the medication alone.3Although these treatments may be associated with complete remission and improvement for many patients, they also have been reported to have no effect for others.1,3 Histologically, sebaceous adenitis is characterized by dense neutrophilic inflammation that is centered around the sebaceous unit. Infectious studies are negative, and no viral cytopathic change is present. The diagnosis requires clinical correlation. The differential diagnosis of vulvar sebaceous adenitis includes hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), HSV, vulvar syringomas, and hidradenoma papilliferum. Histopathological examination and HSV PCR are helpful at narrowing the differential diagnosis. HS clinically presents as recurrent inflamed nodules, abscesses, and fistulae that occur on hair-bearing skin of the axillary, inguinal, inframammary, vulvar, and gluteal regions. HS is diagnosed clinically, and histologic confirmation is typically unnecessary. However, if performed, histology of HS is characterized by follicular hyperkeratosis and subsequent inflammation of apocrine glands.5A key distinguishing clinical feature between HS and vulvar sebaceous adenitis is the anatomical location affected: HS occurs on the hair-bearing aspect of the labia majora, while vulvar sebaceous adenitis occurs on the mucosal surfaces of the labia majora and labia minora. Genital HSV is an infection that typically presents with painful vesicles or erosions on the anogenital area. The virus can remain dormant and shed asymptomatically or recur as outbreaks during the individual’s lifetime. There are numerous ways to test for HSV, with PCR being the standard molecular diagnosis technique. Histology results show vesicle formation with viral cytopathic change, multinucleated giant cells, molding of cells together, and chromatin margination.6 Syringomas are benign adnexal tumors that present as flesh-colored papules. The papules most commonly occur periorbitally, but also rarely occur on the vulva. The lesions may be pruritic or asymptomatic and are thus found incidentally. Vulvar syringomas are diagnosed via skin biopsy specimens, with microscopy revealing sweat ductlike glandular structures.7Symptomatic presentation of tenderness and cyclical patterns are key clinical characteristics that distinguish vulvar sebaceous adenitis from vulvar syringomas.
